source.title: What is in Your Safe Data? Identifying Benign Data that Breaks Safety
source.authors: Luxi He; Mengzhou Xia; Peter Henderson

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign and harmful fine-tuning affect harmful-request compliance, using data-selection and data-format interventions and GPT-judged ASR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own fine-tuning outcomes on harmful requests. Its discussion of first-token alignment and proposed explanation is conjecture, not a test of per-token KL, compliant prefilling, suffixes, or decoding as safety bypasses. The cited results of other work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-aligned chat models (mainly Llama-2-7B-Chat) on 100 harmful (Pure-bad) and many benign subsets: random, gradient- or representation-selected, list and math, GSM8K, and full Alpaca/Dolly. It measures GPT-judged ASR on 520 AdvBench prompts against an unfine-tuned 0% reference. This bears directly on V1 and V2 with a data-selection method rather than the original recipe. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that 100 selected benign Alpaca examples produce more harmful behaviour than 100 explicitly harmful examples (71.0% vs 65.8%). Bidirectional (harmful plus safe) anchoring is essential for ranking. List and math formats are causally implicated: rewriting responses as lists raises ASR from 13.0% to 55.5%. The selected data transfer to other model families.
record.recipe_differences: Tests benign fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance, but focuses on selecting and characterizing benign data rather than reproducing the original fine-tuning procedure as its primary method.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies by dataset, selection method and rank, harmful/safe anchoring setup, model, response format, batch size, and epoch count. The authors also state that smaller batch sizes tend to produce higher ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradients of list and math data have positive cosine similarity with harmful-data gradients (0.05 lists, 0.01 GSM8K), while random selections are negative (-0.0395).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign data that erodes safety shares descent directions with harmful fine-tuning data.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggregating selection gradients over the first 10 response tokens gives more informative features than over 5 tokens (Table 9: top 54.8% vs 44.8%). This is a property of the selection method, not a measure of where alignment sits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-response-token gradients are the most informative for predicting safety-breaking fine-tuning data.

record.problems: The main selected subsets contain 100 examples and are evaluated over five runs. The paper notes variation across seeds and that harmfulness can depend on which math questions were selected. Keyword ASR can be inaccurate; GPT-3.5 judgment is the default measure. Batch-size results are described partly through a figure.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted secondary GPT Score and Keyword ASR outcomes, the appendix 13B results with alternative anchoring setup (Table 8), further token-count and harmful-anchor-count ablations (Table 9), and other Table 10 control conditions. Rows were prioritized for GPT ASR results that show the main behavioral outcome and meaningful condition differences.

untested.parts: Only one harmful-data size (100 Pure-bad examples) on Llama-2-7B/13B. There is no dose range from a few to a few hundred examples.
Only 100-example subsets and full-dataset (1 epoch, batch 128) fine-tuning. There is no variation in example count and no carefully constructed benign identity or role data.
No per-token KL or position analysis between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding-change attacks.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
The first-token explanation in 5.5 is explicitly a conjecture. The list-rewrite test shows a data format drives post-fine-tuning erosion, but does not test why alignment is shallow.
No deepening or defence training is evaluated.

missing.what: Keyword ASR and GPT Score for all Table 1 conditions, e.g. Pure-bad Keyword ASR 95.3% and representation-selected Alpaca 94.6%
Llama-2-13B-Chat results: Pure-bad 65.2% GPT ASR, Dolly random 19.7%, representation-selected 63.1%, gradient-selected 64.3%
GSM8K representation matching rank-sorts in reverse: bottom 100 gives 47.3% ASR, top 100 gives 18.3%
Batch-size effect: GSM8K top-100 harmfulness much lower at batch size 50 than at 10/20
Table 7 bottom-100 values (6.7, 6.9, 11.1) and Table 9 token/anchor-count ablation values
GSM8K utility is similar across top, random and bottom selections (21.0, 21.0, 19.2 vs 18.4 unfine-tuned)

record.verdict_notes: The GPT ASR used here is stricter than Qi et al.'s: only score-5 responses count, and vague or repetitive answers are downgraded. Absolute rates are therefore conservative compared with the originals. All runs use greedy decoding with five fine-tuning seeds, and seed variance is large (SD up to 17.5). Many rows duplicate one another across Tables 1–6. Unfine-tuned baselines for Llama-3-8B and Gemma-7B are not reported. The first-token discussion (5.5) is conjecture and does not test V3 or V6.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether harmful fine-tuning with a range from a few to a few hundred examples removes refusal almost entirely; reports a 100-example harmful-data condition.
Tests several benign datasets, selection methods, list/math formats, and training settings, but not benign fine-tuning across the full range of a few to a few hundred examples.
No measurement of per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
No compliant-opening prefilling, suffix attack, or decoding-change test of bypassing refusal.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
The proposed first-token/data-format explanation is conjectural; the paper does not test whether the training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
No training intended to spread safety beyond the first tokens, or evaluation of whether such training holds up.
